claim: [SELF-STORAGE] NIBRS hotel rule allows "up to 99 units per event", cited to the Modern Storage Media survey article
problem: The cited article does not contain the 99 figure and does not name NIBRS; it says only that a 20-unit break-in is often treated as a single burglary. The 99 cap is real (it is the NIBRS Number of Premises Entered field limit per the FBI NIBRS user manual), but it is not in the cited source, so the number is unsupported at that URL.
fix: Either drop "up to 99 units" or re-cite it to the FBI NIBRS user manual (Number of Premises Entered, 01-99) and keep the MSM article only for the hotel-rule description.

claim: [GYMS] "attending at least once in a month was associated with a ~20% lower likelihood of cancelling" (Rand et al., 2020, doi 10.1016/j.psychsport.2020.101771)
problem: Not supported by the cited study. The paper analyses 1,726 new members on 12-month contracts that cannot be cancelled during their term; it reports attendance decline (7.48 visits in month 1 to 0.92 in month 12) and the share attending at least once (100% to 22%), plus correlates of fourth-quarter attendance. It reports no cancellation rates and no ~20% figure.
fix: Delete the cancellation clause, or replace it with what the paper actually says: 7.48 -> 0.92 mean visits and 100% -> 22% attending at least once by month 12.

claim: N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 "makes it a crime to observe or record another person where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed"
problem: Overstated legal rule. The statute is narrower: it criminalises observing/photographing another person where a reasonable person would know the other may expose intimate parts or engage in sexual penetration or sexual contact, without consent, in circumstances where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed. The affirmative defense (prior posted notice plus lawful purpose) attaches to that conduct, not to video surveillance generally.
fix: Restate as an intimate-parts/sexual-activity privacy offence that requires excluding restrooms, changing areas and locker rooms, and stop presenting it as a general reasonable-expectation-of-privacy recording ban; keep the posted-notice point as practice, not as a general statutory defense.

claim: Rhombus pricing: "MSRP $399 (R120 dome) + $149 license = $548 per camera; higher models to $1,699 + license"

fix: Say "$548 per camera for the R120; most models $748-$1,948 with licence; multi-sensor R600 about $3,948".
